assessment_summary: This paper reports a purposive expert survey (N=51/92 invited) eliciting agreement with 50 proposed AGI-lab safety and governance practices. Strengths include clear scope, preregistration and OSF materials, transparent item/figure reporting, high response rate, and appropriate nonparametric tests with multiple-comparisons correction. Key limitations: (i) small, networked, non-representative sampling (overlap with AGI labs and safety community) risks selection and self-selection bias; (ii) items are abstract, normative, and framed as “should,” inviting acquiescence/social-desirability and inflating agreement; (iii) optional items yield varying n and comparability; (iv) means on ordinal Likert data and across heterogeneous items; (v) limited robustness checks (no nonresponse analysis, alternative phrasings, randomized item order, or weighting); (vi) low power for subgroup tests—null item-level differences are weak evidence; (vii) extrapolation from opinions to “best practices” is not validated by outcomes; (viii) some data withheld for anonymity constrains full replication of subgroup analyses. Overall, the study credibly characterizes preferences within this sample but should avoid generalizing to a broad expert consensus or to practice effectiveness without further evidence.

Pantropical 30 m mapping of biophysical potential for natural regeneration is trained on observed 2000–2016 regrowth and predicts ~215 Mha and 23.4 Gt C over 30 years. Strengths: uses realized regrowth rather than assumed suitability; clear variable selection; relationships (proximity to forest, local forest density, soil C) have strong ecological plausibility. Key limitations: training labels depend on global regrowth/plantation discrimination with known omission in humid forests; the liberal sampling domain and omission errors introduce label noise. Validation reports overall “accuracy” on balanced random points; despite a distance-to-training diagnostic, there is no formal spatial block cross-validation, AUC/precision–recall, or probability calibration; results may be optimistic and probabilities miscalibrated, affecting the expected-area calculation. Several predictors are coarser than 30 m, potentially imprinting coarse patterns; socioeconomic drivers were excluded from predictions, so maps reflect biophysical potential and may overestimate feasible restoration. Carbon estimates downscale 1-km rates uniformly and do not propagate uncertainty or leakage/additionality risks; very narrow CIs on area reflect numerical, not model, uncertainty. Data products are openly hosted, but full code is “on request” and some proprietary workflows reduce reproducibility.

Strong, policy-relevant geo-randomized field experiment covering 7,686 German postal codes with a 2x2 factorial design (video content; impression allocation). Major strengths: near-national scope, preregistration, blocking on predicted potential, intention-to-treat analysis using all-channel donation outcomes, and multiple robustness checks (DiD, randomization inference). Main outcome (revenue) is modest and borderline significant; frequency effects are clearer. Key limitations: (i) outcomes aggregated at PLZ-day and normalized per capita—this equal-weights PLZs and may differ from population-weighted effects; (ii) variation in ad exposure within treated PLZs implies ITT, potentially attenuating effects; (iii) winsorization at €1,000 and trimming extreme-reach PLZs affect external validity; (iv) some donation records may lack postal codes; differential missingness by treatment is untested; (v) spillover estimates using “share of treated neighbors” are suggestive but could be confounded by spatial sorting; magnitudes seem large relative to direct effects; (vi) evidence on crowding out relies partly on online-only competitor data and exhibits pretreatment imbalance (addressed with DiD but still noisy); (vii) ROI hinges on an assumed donor lifetime multiplier (1.75) and excludes some downstream costs; (viii) multiple heterogeneity tests lack multiplicity adjustment. Replicability is constrained by proprietary data; preregistration helps but full code/data availability is unclear.

This is a timely, well-scoped systematic review and RVE meta-analysis synthesizing 1,307 effects from 93 RCTs on social safety nets (SSNs) and women’s outcomes across 45 LMICs. Strengths include clear inclusion criteria, broad SSN coverage beyond cash transfers, use of Hedges’ g with small-sample correction, clustered inference via robust variance estimation, multiple sensitivity checks, and transparent acknowledgement of heterogeneity. Key limitations: very high between-study heterogeneity (I2 ~80–95%) with limited explanatory power of moderators; pooling diverse constructs (economic and agency) risks interpretational ambiguity; outcome standardization choices (handling of binary outcomes, indices, and potential double-counting when including both component measures and aggregate indices) are not fully documented; currency valuation of benefit size in nominal USD without PPP/duration normalization may attenuate design insights; meta-regressions separated by level raise omitted-variable risks; several internal numerical inconsistencies (e.g., public works effect 0.127 vs 0.273; a decision-making CI appears mis-typed) reduce confidence; publication bias assessment not described in detail; only RCTs included, limiting generalizability; cost-benefit synthesis is non-standardized and rarely incorporates women-specific benefits; replication files promised but data extraction form not public. Despite these issues, conclusions—small positive, policy-relevant effects, stronger for UCTs/assets/care, weaker for CCTs/in-kind—are broadly credible.
